title: A thread of oil
hookLine: oil poured from a jar falls in one unbroken thread, and Ramanuja says that is what knowing God looks like
carry: bhakti: knowing god, remembered without a break

cards: Tip a jar of oil, slowly, over a bowl. It doesn't splash or scatter. It falls in one thin, glossy thread, unbroken from the lip of the jar to the bowl below.
Ramanuja reaches for that thread in the opening pages of the Sri Bhashya, when he asks a plain question. The Upanishads promise freedom to the one who knows Brahman. But what kind of knowing?
Reading a sentence and nodding? Understanding it once, on a good afternoon? His answer is the thread of oil.

teach.b: The Upanishads use more than one word for this knowing: know, meditate, worship. Ramanuja argues they mean the same thing, and that it isn't a one-time flash of understanding.
It's meditation that keeps going, a remembering of God that doesn't break, like oil poured in a steady stream.

His key phrase comes from the Chandogya Upanishad: when one's food, the things taken in, is pure, the mind becomes pure; when the mind is pure, remembrance becomes firm; and with firm remembrance, every knot comes loose.
Dhruva smriti: firm, steady remembrance. Then a step further. Remembered steadily enough, he says, it becomes so vivid that it's like seeing.

teach.h: KNOWING THAT DOESN'T STOP IS LOVE.
teach.b: And remembrance that is like seeing, and full of love, is what the Upanishads call knowing. That's bhakti. So for Ramanuja, devotion isn't a softer path beside knowledge.
It's what knowledge becomes when it doesn't stop. One more turn. The Katha Upanishad says the self isn't gained by teaching or cleverness, but by the one it chooses.
Who gets chosen? Ramanuja answers: the one who has become dearest, through this unbroken loving remembrance. Knowing, loving and being chosen run together, like one thread.
The Alvars sang this; Ramanuja argues it, line by line.

teach.h: WHY THE NAME IS SAID AGAIN.
teach.b: And it's why so much Hindu practice is repetition: a name said on a mala, a hundred and eight times, the same hymn every morning. Not because the words are forgotten, but because the thread isn't meant to break.

how: Sri Vaishnavas cultivate steady remembrance of Vishnu through daily worship, japa of his names on a mala (often the eight-syllable Om Namo Narayanaya), recitation of the Alvar hymns, and quiet meditation; teachers point to Ramanuja's image of oil poured in an unbroken stream.

o: the old songs sung at Vishnu's festivals each year
careful thought about Vishnu, the God you can love
the rules priests follow in Vishnu's temples each day

games.q: the thread of oil: tap the pairs.
p: so vivid it's like direct sight
the one who has become dearest

s: for Ramanuja, knowing Brahman is a single flash of insight
he reads it as meditation that keeps going, unbroken like oil poured.
Ramanuja says steady, loving remembrance is bhakti
knowing that doesn't stop becomes love.
the Chandogya links a pure mind to firm remembrance
and with firm remembrance, every knot comes loose.

games.q: the Upanishads promise freedom to the one who knows Brahman. you're Ramanuja. what kind of knowing do you say they mean?
o: remembrance that never breaks, full of love.
games.why: Ramanuja reads it as unbroken remembrance, like oil poured, so vivid it's like seeing: and that, he says, is bhakti.

practice: If you pray, take the name you pray to; many Sri Vaishnavas use the eight-syllable mantra, Om Namo Narayanaya. Say it slowly, again and again, letting it flow like oil from a tipped jar.
If you don't pray, hold a face you love, or simply the breath. When the thread breaks, don't scold yourself; just tip the jar again and let it start over.

wordCard.voice: Vaishnava theology. Today, knowing God as dhruva smriti: steady remembrance, poured like oil, so vivid it's like seeing, and full of love. That's bhakti.

orig.note: Sanskrit: firm remembrance, from the Chandogya Upanishad, which Ramanuja reads as the knowing that frees.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti: knowing God, remembered without a break. A thread of oil, poured and poured again. See you tomorrow.
